Growthbook is awesome! We have used the self-hosted version a few months in my company now, and are very happy about it. Talented people behind it, and issues are resolved quickly.

Been using GrowthBook for a few weeks now... I was shocked at how much setup time it took to get a simple feature flag into our app with other services like Darkly. We had Growthbook working in roughly 15 minutes with under 10 lines of code changed.

BoldVoice has been using GrowthBook for about ~6 weeks or so now, and it was super lucky that we found these guys right as we were considering way more expensive options like Optimizely (...6 figures). The tooling is pretty intuitive and support has been stellar.
At Miggos we have implemented Growth book and we got FF and A/B in our Vue frontend in a few hours. Excited to see the progress of the platform.

Re: Eppo - they're similar in setup but Growthbook is open source with an optional cloud SaaS offering. Optimizely is a walled garden, you need to push all your metrics as events; Eppo and GrowthBook both connect to your data warehouse instead.

With GrowthBook, there's a single cacheable JSON definition of all of the features and then evaluation happens locally within the SDKs... The other missing part in most feature flagging tools is the analysis side... We built that part directly into GrowthBook.

There's definitely a gap in GrowthBook right now... between pure feature flags and experiments. We're working on some light-weight event tracking features to try and bridge that gap, to see how many people are using features and integrate with DataDog/NewRelic.
a guide in your docs on how to use this with Matomo would go far. Growthbook provides Feature Flag and A/B Testing, but you have to bring your own analytics.

Isn't running many experiments in parallel a bad practice in general? Not only you split your (potentially limited) sample count, but it is very unlikely that there is ZERO interaction between A/B tests.
We're using MongoDB to store cached A/B test results... which are deeply nested JSON objects. MongoDB let us develop features really quickly so it's been a great choice so far for us.

From the looks of it, it doesn't look like the configuration can be stored in the code repository itself. This is one of the key things to do - treating configuration as code and properly versioning it.
We use a Bayesian statistics engine which is much more immune to peeking problems and Type I errors than frequentist approaches.

We don't have native mobile SDKs yet, but it's something we want to support in the future. Mobile is a little tricky since you either need to do a new release every time you want to start/stop a test or use remote config.
Coupling metrics to experimentation is a huge red flag. You should offload that onto DBT or some other data modeling tools.

A user says their company has run the self-hosted GrowthBook for a few months and is very happy with it, and that issues get resolved quickly. They like that it works on top of existing customer data. They just exposed views over their click-stream data instead of sending data to third parties.
A user had previously struggled to build an internal A/B testing tool. At Miggos they implemented GrowthBook and got feature flags and A/B tests into their Vue frontend in a few hours.

Downside raised: GrowthBook provides feature flags and A/B testing, but you have to bring your own analytics. The user notes a GitHub issue about Matomo integration had been open since September with no docs guide or SQL examples.

Comparison: Optimizely is a walled garden where you must push all metrics as events to it. GrowthBook (like Eppo) connects to your existing data warehouse and supports any metric you can express as a query. Unlike Eppo, GrowthBook is open source with an optional cloud SaaS.

A user asked whether GrowthBook will support gradual "Feature Rollouts" with metric monitoring like Statsig's feature gates and pulse metrics. Their point: with plain flags you build your own logging and analysis, while full experiments are overly constrained by statistical rigor.
A user wanted a way to self-host GrowthBook without the packaged Docker version, so it could run on shared hosting (uberspace) that doesn't support Docker.
A former Sixpack user says SeatGeek upgraded Sixpack internally to "Sevenpack", but "something like GrowthBook looks much nicer!"

Complaint about the MongoDB dependency: one user said it would be a decently large operational addition to their stack and that a SQL server should suffice. Another said they would likely evaluate and use the product only if it didn't depend on MongoDB, citing its non-open-source SSPL license and reputation.

An A/B experimenter questioned email alerts sent when "significance" is reached. Without minimum sample sizes calculated in advance, they worry this produces Type I errors and leads lay users to believe short tests are statistically sound.
A maintainer of open-source A/B tools (Alephbet), built out of frustration with Optimizely, called GrowthBook "very polished." They noted statistical analysis was always the hardest part for them.

A user found little detail on how GrowthBook handles multi-armed bandit and early-stopping problems beyond Bayesian stats with unknown priors. They also worry that drilling down by categories makes significance even more of a concern.

One company has used the self-hosted version for a few months and is very happy with it; issues get resolved quickly. They like that it runs on top of existing customer data. They expose views over their own click-stream data, so they keep one high-quality data source instead of sending data to third-party tools and handling many data processing agreements.

A small startup (Ping Labs) using it for a few weeks: other services like LaunchDarkly took a surprising amount of setup time for a simple feature flag. They had GrowthBook working in roughly 15 minutes with under 10 lines of code changed.

BoldVoice has used GrowthBook for about 6 weeks. They found it while considering far more expensive options like Optimizely (six figures). The user calls the tooling pretty intuitive and the founders' support stellar, but says there is still a ton left to build.
At Miggos they had previously struggled to build an internal A/B testing tool. With GrowthBook they got feature flags and A/B tests into their Vue frontend in a few hours.

GrowthBook provides feature flags and A/B testing, but you have to bring your own analytics. One user asked for a docs guide with SQL examples for using it with self-hosted Matomo, noting a GitHub issue on that integration had been open since September.
One user asked whether it can be self-hosted without the Docker package, so it could run on shared hosting (Uberspace) that doesn't support Docker.

One user wished for Statsig-style 'Feature Rollouts'. With plain feature flags, teams must build their own logging and analysis. With experiments, they are overly constrained because experiments are meant to be statistically rigorous.

Criticism of GrowthBook's recommendation to run many A/B tests in parallel: it splits a potentially limited sample, and it is very unlikely there is zero interaction between tests, even when they are on different pages.
Comparison: one commenter is a happy PostHog user instead, since PostHog also supports experimentation and feature flags alongside product analytics.

Critique of the earlier Show HN version: configuration apparently can't be stored in the code repository. The commenter sees treating configuration as code (versioning it, blaming it) as key, though otherwise it 'looks great'.
A regular A/B experimenter questioned the email alerts sent when 'significance' is reached. Without minimum sample sizes calculated in advance, they worry this produces many Type 1 errors.
One commenter called coupling metrics to experimentation 'a huge red flag' and said metrics should be offloaded to dbt or other data modeling tools.

Statistics concerns: it is unclear how multi-armed bandits and early stopping are handled, beyond Bayesian statistics with unknown priors. Allowing drill-down by various categories would make statistical significance even more of a concern.

A maintainer of open-source A/B tools, built out of frustration with Optimizely, found GrowthBook very polished. They noted statistical analysis is the hardest part and currently rely on the commercial Analytics Toolkit for it.
One commenter questioned the choice of MongoDB as the backing database, citing a negative association with it.
